app/models/blocked_email.rb:17 — Blocked-attempt statistics are saved inside the user save transaction, so rejected email validation rolls back match_count and last_match_at.
app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — The read-modify-save counter update loses match_count increments when concurrent requests read the same value; use an atomic database increment.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core issue: the should_block_email? method has side effects (updating statistics/counters) during what should be a read operation. The golden comment frames this as 'side effects during a read operation' causing race conditions, while the candidate specifically identifies the race condition in the counter update mechanism. Both point to the same problematic behavior - concurrent access issues with the match_count update in a method that's supposed to just check if an email should be blocked.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:17 — Blocked-attempt statistics are saved inside the user save transaction, so rejected email validation rolls back match_count and last_match_at.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: BlockedEmail.should_block? calls record.save (line 15-16 in blocked_email.rb) to update match_count and last_match_at. This method is called from EmailValidator.validate_each during User model validation. If the email is blocked, the validation adds an error, causing the user save to fail and rollback. Since the BlockedEmail.save happens within the same transaction context (during validation of the User model), the statistics update would be rolled back along with the failed user creation. This is a legitimate transactional bug.
